title: 3. Innovation and Disruption
subtitle: Wealth management · Robo advisors · DeFi · Big data · Cryptocurrency · Blockchain
subject: FinTech

sections.heading: Introduction and Learning Objectives
sections.html:
Innovation in finance is moving from digitising existing services to rethinking how value is created and trusted. This module follows an investor's journey through wealth management and robo advice, then explores decentralised finance, big data analytics, cryptocurrency and blockchain, and ends with the tax rules for virtual digital assets in AY 2026-27.

Learning objectives

  • Describe the wealth management process and its digital tools
  • Explain how robo advisors work and their limitations
  • Understand DeFi, big data and social media analytics
  • Trace the evolution of cryptocurrency
  • Explain blockchain basics and its framework
  • Apply AY 2026-27 tax rules to virtual digital assets

sections.heading: 3.1 The Wealth Management Process
sections.html:
Wealth management is the disciplined process of planning, growing and protecting a person's financial resources to meet life goals. It goes beyond buying products: it begins with understanding the client and ends with continuous review. FinTech has digitised and partly automated each step, making professional-style planning affordable to ordinary investors.

1
Profile the client (risk and needs)
→
2
Set goals (education, retirement)
→
3
Allocate assets (equity, debt, gold)
→
4
Implement (buy funds or stocks)
→
5
Monitor and rebalance

Fig. 1. Wealth management process

Client profiling records age, income, dependants, liabilities and, importantly, risk tolerance (emotional comfort with losses) and risk capacity (financial ability to bear losses). Goal setting converts needs into amounts and time horizons, for example Rs 25 lakh for a child's higher education in 12 years. Asset allocation divides money among equity, debt, gold and other assets; it is the main determinant of long-run risk and return, an idea rooted in Markowitz's portfolio theory, which shows that diversification can reduce risk for a given return [1]. Implementation uses mutual funds, stocks, bonds or insurance. Monitoring and rebalancing restores the target mix when market movements drift it.

Behavioural aspects of investing

Investors do not always behave as rational textbook agents. Common biases include loss aversion (feeling losses more than equal gains), herding (following the crowd), overconfidence (trading too much) and recency bias (extrapolating recent returns). Digital platforms can magnify these biases through push notifications, leaderboards and one-tap trading, or reduce them through goal reminders, default SIPs and cooling-off prompts. A responsible wealth management process therefore pays attention to how choices are presented as well as to what is offered.

Common instruments

Table 1. Instruments used in digital wealth management

InstrumentNatureTypical role in a portfolio
Equity shares and equity mutual fundsOwnership in companiesLong-term growth
Debt funds, bonds and depositsLending for interestStability and income
Gold (physical, ETF, sovereign instruments)Store of valueDiversification
Exchange-traded funds and index fundsLow-cost market exposureCore holdings
National Pension System and insuranceRetirement and protectionLong-term security

Indian example: A goal-based plan for a young professional

A 30-year-old software engineer in Chennai with a high risk appetite might hold about 70 per cent equity, 20 per cent debt and 10 per cent gold, invested through monthly Systematic Investment Plans (SIPs), and rebalance once a year. The percentages are illustrative, not advice.

As she nears a goal, the plan gradually shifts from equity to debt to protect accumulated wealth.

sections.heading: 3.2 Platforms, Interfaces and Advantages of Technology
sections.html:
Digital wealth platforms such as Zerodha Coin, Groww and ET Money offer account opening, mutual fund purchase, SIPs, stock trading and goal tracking in one app. Behind the screen sits a chain of system interfaces connected by APIs: the investor app, the broker or asset management company (AMC), the exchange and depositories, and the bank for payments.

1
Investor app
→
2
API layer
→
3
Broker or AMC
→
4
Exchange and depository (NSE, BSE, NSDL, CDSL)
→
5
Bank settlement

Fig. 2. Interfaces behind an investment app

Table 2. Advantages of adopting technology in wealth management

AdvantageExplanationIndian illustration
Lower costFewer intermediaries and automated processesDirect mutual fund plans, available since 2013, carry lower expense ratios than regular plans
Convenience and accessInvest anytime from a phoneSIPs started from small amounts
TransparencyReal-time portfolio and cost visibilityConsolidated account statements
PersonalisationGoal-based recommendations from dataGoal planners in investment apps
ScalabilityOne platform serves millionsLarge retail participation in equity markets

Technology also introduces concerns: over-trading encouraged by gamified interfaces, herd behaviour driven by social media tips, and operational outages during peak volumes. Investor education and regulatory oversight by SEBI remain essential [2].

Revenue models of investment platforms

Platforms earn money in different ways: brokerage on trades, commissions from fund houses for regular plans, subscription fees, or interest on margin funding. Each model creates incentives. A platform paid mainly on trading volume may encourage frequent trading; one paid by subscription is less dependent on volumes. Since 2013, SEBI has required mutual funds to offer direct plans without distributor commission, giving investors a lower-cost route [2]. Students should examine who pays, how much and with what conflict of interest.

Types of interfaces

  • Market data interfaces: deliver live prices and historical data.
  • Order management interfaces: send buy and sell orders to exchanges through brokers.
  • KYC and onboarding interfaces: verify identity through eKYC and CKYC.
  • Payment interfaces: collect funds through UPI or net banking and settle payouts.
  • Reporting interfaces: generate contract notes, statements and tax reports.

Many brokers now offer public trading APIs that allow clients and developers to build their own tools, which opens innovation but also requires safeguards such as authentication, rate limits and risk checks.

sections.heading: 3.3 FinTech Companies and Robo Advisors
sections.html:
A robo advisor is an online platform that provides automated, algorithm-based investment advice or portfolio management with minimal human involvement. The client answers a questionnaire on goals, horizon and risk tolerance; the algorithm proposes a diversified portfolio, usually of low-cost index funds or exchange-traded funds, and rebalances it periodically [3].

Early global examples include Betterment and Wealthfront in the United States. Their value proposition is low fees, low minimum investments and discipline, helped by features such as automatic rebalancing and tax-loss harvesting in some markets. In India, advice is regulated by SEBI's Investment Advisers Regulations, 2013, which require registration and fiduciary conduct [2]; several platforms offer algorithm-assisted, goal-based portfolios within this framework.

Table 3. Robo advisors versus human advisors

DimensionRobo advisorHuman advisor
CostLow, often a small percentage feeHigher, often a larger percentage fee or fixed fee
PersonalisationRule- and questionnaire-basedDeep understanding of family situations
Behavioural coachingLimitedStrong, especially in market panics
Complex needs (estate, business)WeakStrong
Availability24x7By appointment

Types of robo advisors

Table 4. Pure robo, hybrid and execution-only

TypeDescriptionStrengthLimitation
Pure robo advisorFully automated advice and rebalancingLowest costNo human help for complex cases
Hybrid advisorAlgorithm plus human advisersBalance of cost and careHigher fees than pure robo
Execution-only platformAllows the client to trade without adviceFlexibility, low chargesNo suitability assessment

How the algorithm decides

Most robo advisors translate the questionnaire into a risk score and map it to a model portfolio built on portfolio theory, which seeks the best combination of assets for a given level of risk [1]. Some use factor-based or risk-balanced approaches. Rebalancing rules trigger trades when allocations drift beyond tolerance bands, and some platforms harvest tax losses where the law allows [3].

Ethical and regulatory issues

Key questions include suitability (is the advice right for this client?), fiduciary duty (does the adviser act in the client's interest?), transparency (are assumptions and fees disclosed?) and accountability (who is responsible when the algorithm errs?). In India, advisers must be registered under SEBI's Investment Advisers Regulations and follow requirements on risk profiling, suitability and disclosure, so a platform that gives advice must meet these standards [2].

Case study: Robo advisors

Situation. A first-time investor with Rs 5,000 a month wants a diversified portfolio but cannot afford a traditional adviser.

Solution. A robo platform builds a mix of index funds from a risk questionnaire and rebalances it annually.

Outcome and limits. The investor gets disciplined, low-cost investing. However, if the investor panics during a market fall, a purely algorithmic service may not provide the reassurance a human would. Hybrid models, combining algorithms with human advice, aim to capture both strengths.

sections.heading: 3.4 Decentralized Finance (DeFi)
sections.html:
Decentralized Finance refers to financial services such as trading, lending and borrowing that run on public blockchains using smart contracts, which are programs that execute automatically when conditions are met, rather than through banks or brokers [4], [5].

Key building blocks include decentralised exchanges (DEXs), where users trade tokens directly from wallets; stablecoins, tokens designed to hold a stable value by reference to a currency; lending protocols, where users deposit crypto as collateral to borrow; and liquidity pools, pools of tokens that allow automated trading and reward providers with fees (sometimes called yield farming). Oracles feed external information, such as prices, to smart contracts.

Table 5. Opportunities and risks of DeFi

OpportunitiesRisks
Open, 24x7 accessSmart-contract bugs and hacks
Transparency of code and transactionsExtreme volatility and liquidation
Programmable, composable servicesLittle or no consumer protection or recourse
Lower intermediary costsRegulatory and tax uncertainty

From an Indian regulatory perspective, DeFi activity involving virtual digital assets is subject to tax rules described later in this module and to evolving oversight, so participation carries legal and financial risk.

The layers of the DeFi stack

Schär describes DeFi as a layered system built on a blockchain base [4]. At the bottom is the settlement layer, the blockchain and its native asset. Above it lies the asset layer of tokens, including stablecoins. The protocol layer contains smart-contract standards for trading, lending and derivatives; the application layer provides user-friendly front ends; and the aggregation layer combines services, for example by finding the best price across exchanges. The ability to combine protocols like building blocks is called composability, and it can also spread failures quickly.

Table 6. Centralised finance versus decentralised finance

AspectCentralised finance (CeFi)Decentralised finance (DeFi)
IntermediaryBank, broker or exchangeSmart contracts
AccessAccount and KYC requiredWallet-based, often pseudonymous
CustodyInstitution holds assetsUser holds keys
RecourseComplaint and legal remediesLimited; code is the rule
RegulationLicensing and supervisionUnclear or evolving

In the Indian context, participation in DeFi involves virtual digital assets, so tax rules apply, and users receive no deposit insurance or regulatory recourse. DeFi is best studied as an experiment from which traditional finance may borrow ideas such as programmability and transparency.

sections.heading: 3.5 Social Media Analytics and Big Data
sections.html:
Big data refers to data sets so large, fast or varied that conventional tools cannot process them. Gandomi and Haider describe the commonly cited characteristics, often called the Vs: volume (scale), velocity (speed of generation), variety (structured and unstructured forms), veracity (quality and trustworthiness) and value (usefulness for decisions) [6].

In finance, big-data tools support credit scoring for thin-file customers who lack formal histories, real-time fraud monitoring, customer segmentation and product pricing. Social media analytics applies text mining and sentiment analysis to posts, news and search trends to gauge public mood about companies, markets or products; asset managers use such signals as one input among many. Technologies such as distributed storage and processing frameworks make it possible to analyse these data at scale.

Indian example: Reading mood around a festive-season launch

A consumer-finance company analyses thousands of public posts and reviews during Diwali offers. A rise in negative sentiment about app downtime prompts it to scale up servers and issue a clarification quickly.

The analytics process

1
Collect data from many sources
→
2
Store and clean it
→
3
Analyse with models
→
4
Visualise insights
→
5
Act and monitor outcomes

Fig. 3. Big data analytics process in finance

Techniques include clustering to segment customers, classification to predict default or churn, text mining to extract themes from news and complaints, and network analysis to detect linked accounts in fraud rings [6]. Alternative data such as GST filings, UPI transaction patterns and utility payments broaden the information available for credit decisions.

Ethics and limits

  • Consent and purpose limitation: data should be used only for the purpose for which consent was given [7].
  • Bias: historical data may encode discrimination; models need fairness testing.
  • Manipulation: social media signals can be gamed through bots or coordinated posts.
  • Explainability: customers and regulators need to understand major decisions.

Caution

Social data can be noisy, manipulated or unrepresentative, and its use must respect consent and privacy law [7]. Models trained on biased data can reproduce bias in credit decisions.

sections.heading: 3.6 Cryptocurrency: Evolution
sections.html:
A cryptocurrency is a digital asset that uses cryptography to secure transactions and control the creation of units, typically without a central issuer. The modern era began with the white paper published under the name Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008, proposing a peer-to-peer electronic cash system that solves the double-spending problem without a trusted third party [8]. The Bitcoin network started in January 2009 and its supply is capped at 21 million units; new coins are issued to miners who validate transactions through Proof of Work.

1
2008–09 Bitcoin paper and network
→
2
2015 Ethereum adds smart contracts
→
3
2017–18 ICO boom and bust
→
4
2020 onwards DeFi, NFTs, stablecoins, CBDC pilots

Fig. 4. Evolution of cryptocurrency

Ethereum, introduced in 2015, generalised the idea by allowing programmable smart contracts [5]. The 2017–18 period saw a boom in Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs), many of which failed. Later years brought decentralised finance, non-fungible tokens (NFTs), stablecoins and, from central banks, CBDC pilots [9]. In India, the RBI cautioned against private cryptocurrencies, a banking restriction imposed in 2018 was set aside by the Supreme Court in 2020, and the Finance Act, 2022 introduced a tax regime for virtual digital assets. Cryptocurrency is not legal tender in India.

Types of crypto assets

Table 7. Classification of crypto assets

TypeDescriptionExample
Cryptocurrency (coins)Native asset of a blockchain used as money or for feesBitcoin, Ether
StablecoinsTokens that aim to hold a stable valueTokens pegged to a currency
Utility and governance tokensGive access to a service or voting rightsProtocol tokens
Non-fungible tokens (NFTs)Unique digital itemsDigital art, collectibles
CBDCDigital form of sovereign currency issued by a central bankDigital rupee pilot

Crypto versus CBDC. A cryptocurrency is typically issued by a decentralised network and has no sovereign backing, whereas a CBDC is a liability of the central bank and is legal tender [9]. Their design goals differ: crypto assets emphasise decentralisation, while CBDCs seek efficiency, safety and monetary control.

Exchanges, custody and wallets

Individuals usually buy crypto through exchanges, which match orders and may hold customer assets. Custody risk is a major concern: if an exchange is hacked or fails, customers can lose funds, which is why self-custody in a wallet and proof-of-reserves practices receive attention. Users must also guard private keys and recovery phrases.

India: from restriction to taxation

India's stance has evolved: a banking restriction on dealing with crypto businesses was set aside by the Supreme Court in 2020, the Finance Act, 2022 created a specific tax regime, and later notifications brought certain crypto service providers under anti-money-laundering obligations. Cryptocurrency remains neither legal tender nor prohibited, a position that demands caution from investors [10].

sections.heading: 3.7 Blockchain: Basics and Framework
sections.html:
A blockchain is a distributed, append-only ledger maintained by many computers (nodes) that agree on its contents through a consensus mechanism. Transactions are grouped into blocks; each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, so altering history would require changing every later block, which is practically infeasible. This property is called immutability [11].

1
Transaction created and signed
→
2
Broadcast to network
→
3
Validated by consensus
→
4
Added to a block
→
5
Chain updated

Fig. 5. How a blockchain transaction settles

Consensus mechanisms. In Proof of Work, nodes compete to solve a computational puzzle; it is secure but energy-intensive. In Proof of Stake, validators are chosen according to the tokens they stake, using far less energy. Public blockchains are open to anyone, while permissioned blockchains, such as Hyperledger-based networks, restrict participation and suit consortia of banks and companies.

Table 8. Layered framework of a blockchain system

LayerFunctionExample
NetworkPeer-to-peer nodes propagate dataBitcoin or Ethereum nodes
ConsensusAgreement on valid transactionsProof of Work, Proof of Stake
DataBlocks, hashes and transactionsSHA-256 hashing
Smart contractProgrammable business logicEthereum contracts
ApplicationUser-facing servicesWallets, DeFi apps, supply-chain tracking

Wallets and keys. Ownership is controlled by a private key; a hot wallet is connected to the internet, while a cold wallet is kept offline for stronger security. Losing the private key generally means losing the asset.

Inside a block

Each block holds a header and a list of transactions. The header typically contains a timestamp, a fingerprint (hash) of the previous block, a summary of the transactions and, in Proof-of-Work systems, a number called a nonce that miners vary until the block's hash meets a difficulty target. Since the hash changes completely if even a single character of the data changes, any tampering is immediately detectable [8].

Smart contracts in action

1
Farmer buys cover; rules are coded
→
2
Oracle reports rainfall data
→
3
Contract checks the rule
→
4
Payout released automatically

Fig. 6. A parametric insurance smart contract

Use cases and limitations

Table 9. Blockchain use cases and limitations

Use caseBenefit
Trade finance and letters of creditShared records reduce reconciliation and fraud
Land records and certificatesTamper-resistant history
Cross-border paymentsFaster settlement with fewer intermediaries
Supply chain tracingTransparent provenance of goods

Limitations include scalability (limited transactions per second on some networks), energy use in Proof of Work, privacy (public ledgers expose transaction data), governance (who decides upgrades?) and legal certainty (how smart-contract outcomes are enforced in court). A blockchain is not always the right tool; if a trusted central database works well, adding a blockchain may only add cost [11].

Indian example: Beyond cryptocurrency

Banks and exporters have piloted blockchain platforms for trade documents and syndicated lending to reduce reconciliation and fraud. The same technology can record land titles or certificate issuance so that records cannot be quietly altered.

sections.heading: 3.8 Taxation of Virtual Digital Assets: Assessment Year 2026-27
sections.html:
This section is updated for Assessment Year (AY) 2026-27, which relates to income earned in Financial Year 2025-26 and is assessed under the Income-tax Act, 1961. The Income-tax Act, 2025 applies from 1 April 2026 and replaces the concepts of previous year and assessment year with a single Tax Year, so students should check the transition provisions for later years. The following is a summary of the position stated by the Income Tax Department; readers should verify the latest rules [10].

Table 10. Tax treatment of virtual digital assets (VDAs), AY 2026-27

IssuePosition
Tax on income from transfer of VDAFlat 30 per cent under Section 115BBH, plus applicable surcharge and cess
DeductionsOnly the cost of acquisition is allowed; no other expense
Loss from VDACannot be set off against any other income
Tax deducted at source1 per cent under Section 194S on transfer, subject to thresholds
Return reportingSchedule VDA in the income-tax return
Gift of VDATaxable in the recipient's hands above the prescribed limit
Legal statusNot legal tender in India

Good practice for investors in virtual digital assets

  • Maintain a record of each purchase and sale, with dates, amounts and platform statements.
  • Reconcile platform records with the tax statements that reflect TDS deducted, and report income in the schedule meant for virtual digital assets.
  • Remember that only cost of acquisition is deductible and losses cannot be set off against other income [10].
  • Use regulated platforms, enable two-factor authentication and protect private keys.
  • Review the latest Finance Act and notifications each year, since rules can change.

Common misconceptions

Misconception: crypto is tax-free if not converted to rupees. In fact, transfer includes exchanging one asset for another. Misconception: losses reduce tax on salary. Losses from these assets cannot be set off against other income. Misconception: no tax is due if the platform deducted TDS. TDS is only an advance credit; the total tax liability is computed in the return.

Indian example: Worked illustration

Priya buys a crypto asset for Rs 1,00,000 and sells it for Rs 1,40,000 in FY 2025-26. Gain: Rs 40,000. Tax at 30 per cent: Rs 12,000. Health and education cess at 4 per cent adds Rs 480, giving Rs 12,480 (surcharge ignored). The platform deducts 1 per cent TDS on Rs 1,40,000, that is Rs 1,400, which she claims as credit in her return. A loss on another crypto trade cannot reduce this gain.

sections.heading: 3.9 Innovation and Disruption: Conceptual Frameworks
sections.html:
The title of this module pairs two ideas that are often used loosely. Innovation is the introduction of a new or significantly improved product, process or business model. Disruption, in the sense used by Christensen, describes how a new entrant, often starting with a simpler, cheaper product for overlooked customers, gradually improves and displaces established leaders [12].

Table 11. Sustaining versus disruptive innovation in finance

AspectSustaining innovationDisruptive innovation
Target customersExisting, demanding customersOverlooked or new customers
PerformanceBetter on traditional measuresInitially simpler; better on convenience or price
Who leadsIncumbentsEntrants
ExampleBank adds a mobile app to its existing accountsSmall-ticket digital lending to first-time borrowers

Incumbent responses. Established institutions can respond by acquiring or partnering with entrants, building separate digital units, or lowering costs. Policy responses. Regulators attempt to keep markets contestable while ensuring that new models do not compromise stability or consumers [13]. A helpful test for any new product is to ask whether it truly lowers cost or widens access or merely repackages an existing service.

Indian example: Mobile payments and card networks

Card payments were built for a world of card readers and larger purchases. UPI started by serving small, person-to-person payments that cards ignored. As it improved, it moved to merchants and e-commerce, reshaping the payments landscape and showing how a low-end entrant can grow into the mainstream.

Discussion

Is robo advice a disruptive innovation for wealth managers, or a sustaining one that helps them serve more clients? Argue both views.

sections.heading: Chapter Summary
sections.html:
Chapter summary

  • Wealth management follows profiling, goal-setting, allocation, implementation and rebalancing
  • Technology lowers cost and widens access but needs investor education
  • Robo advisors offer scalable, low-cost advice but limited on complex needs
  • DeFi and crypto bring innovation along with high risk and regulatory uncertainty
  • Blockchain's hash-linked ledger enables trust without a central intermediary
  • For AY 2026-27, VDA gains attract a flat 30% tax with 1% TDS and no loss set-off

sections.heading: Review Questions
sections.html:
The questions follow the revised Bloom's taxonomy (Remember, Understand, Apply, Analyse, Evaluate, Create); the level is shown in italics after each question. Answer each in your own words, using the module and the Indian examples.

Short answer questions

  1. List the steps in the wealth management process. (Remember)
  2. Define robo advisor and decentralised finance. (Remember)
  3. State the five Vs of big data. (Remember)
  4. Explain asset allocation and rebalancing. (Understand)
  5. Explain how a blockchain achieves immutability. (Understand)
  6. Distinguish between Proof of Work and Proof of Stake. (Understand)
  7. Explain what a stablecoin is and how it differs from a central bank digital currency. (Understand)
  8. A young professional wants goal-based investing through an app. Illustrate how the interfaces behind the app support her from onboarding to settlement. (Apply)
  9. An investor made a gain on one crypto asset and a loss on another in FY 2025-26. Explain the treatment of the loss and the role of TDS for AY 2026-27. (Apply)
  10. Differentiate between pure robo advisors, hybrid advisors and execution-only platforms. (Analyse)

Long answer questions

  1. Analyse the wealth management process and evaluate how technology changes each step. (Analyse)
  2. Using the robo advisor case, evaluate the suitability of robo advice for a small investor, discussing strengths, limitations and regulatory and ethical issues. (Evaluate)
  3. Analyse the layers of the DeFi stack, compare DeFi with centralised finance and assess its risks. (Analyse)
  4. Discuss how big data and social media analytics are used in finance and examine the ethical limits on their use. (Analyse)
  5. Evaluate the evolution of cryptocurrency and its regulatory and tax position in India. Should it be treated as a mainstream investment? Justify your answer. (Evaluate)
  6. Design a blockchain-based solution for a problem in Indian finance, such as trade finance or certificate verification. Specify the participants, type of blockchain, smart-contract rule and limitations, and relate the idea to the framework of sustaining versus disruptive innovation. (Create)

sections.heading: Glossary
sections.html:
TermMeaning
Wealth managementThe planned process of growing and protecting financial resources to meet life goals.
Asset allocationDivision of investments among asset classes such as equity, debt and gold.
RebalancingRestoring a portfolio to its target asset mix.
SIPSystematic Investment Plan, regular investment of a fixed sum in a fund.
Direct planA mutual fund plan without distributor commission, with a lower expense ratio.
Robo advisorAn automated platform that gives algorithm-based investment advice or portfolio management.
Smart contractA self-executing program on a blockchain that runs when conditions are met.
DeFiDecentralized Finance, financial services run on blockchains through smart contracts.
DEXDecentralised exchange, where users trade tokens directly from wallets.
StablecoinA crypto token designed to hold a stable value by reference to an asset.
Liquidity poolA pool of tokens in a smart contract that enables automated trading.
OracleA service that feeds external data to a smart contract.
Big dataData sets so large, fast or varied that conventional tools cannot handle them.
Sentiment analysisText analysis that measures opinions or mood expressed in content.
CryptocurrencyA digital asset secured by cryptography, usually without a central issuer.
BlockchainA distributed, append-only ledger linked by cryptographic hashes.
HashA fixed-length digital fingerprint computed from data.
Proof of WorkA consensus method in which nodes solve computational puzzles to add blocks.
Proof of StakeA consensus method in which validators are chosen according to tokens they stake.
VDAVirtual Digital Asset, the category used in Indian tax law for crypto assets and similar tokens.
Disruptive innovationInnovation that starts with a simpler or cheaper offering for overlooked customers and later displaces leaders.
